title: How Big a Fiscal Change?
short: Divide the output gap by the right multiplier to find the change in spending or taxes needed.
trouble: Students set the spending change equal to the whole output gap, ignoring the multiplier, or use the spending multiplier for a tax change.

blocks.html: Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy tells you which way to move. The multipliers tell you how far. Because each dollar of new spending is multiplied, the change needed is much smaller than the gap.

To close a gap with government purchases: $\Delta G = \dfrac{\text{gap}}{\text{spending multiplier}}$. With taxes: $\Delta T = \dfrac{\text{gap}}{MPC/MPS}$ (a cut for a recessionary gap, a rise for an inflationary gap). This simple rule assumes the price level stays about the same.

If the multiplier is 5, every \$1 of new government purchases raises GDP by \$5. To raise GDP by \$100 billion, the government needs only \$20 billion: $20 \times 5 = 100$. Setting the change equal to the whole gap would overshoot. For taxes, the multiplier is smaller ($MPC/MPS$, one less), because households save part of a tax cut before spending, so a larger tax change is needed for the same effect.

blocks.name: ec-multiplier
blocks.cap: A \$20 billion rise in purchases with MPC 0.8: the rounds add up toward \$100 billion.

blocks.title: Using government purchases
blocks.q: A recessionary gap is \$200 billion and the MPC is 0.75. How much should government purchases rise?

blocks.title: Using taxes
blocks.q: The same \$200 billion gap, MPC 0.75. How much should taxes be cut?
steps: Tax cut $= \dfrac{200}{3} \approx 66.7$ billion dollars, more than the \$50 billion of purchases.

blocks.title: An inflationary gap
blocks.q: An inflationary gap is \$90 billion and the MPC is 0.9. By how much should purchases fall? Or taxes rise?
steps: Spending multiplier $= 10$: cut purchases by $\dfrac{90}{10} = 9$ billion dollars.
Tax multiplier $= 9$: raise taxes by $\dfrac{90}{9} = 10$ billion dollars.
blocks.a: Cut G by \$9 billion, or raise taxes by \$10 billion

blocks.html: Why "about"? With an upward-sloping SRAS, part of an AD shift goes into a higher price level rather than more output, so in practice a somewhat larger change would be needed. Real-world multipliers are also uncertain, which is one reason economists debate how much fiscal policy to use.

Setting the spending change equal to the whole output gap, ignoring the multiplier, or using the spending multiplier for a tax change. Check: multiply your answer by the right multiplier; you should get back the gap.
